    ← CIA I · Component 1 · Essay 01

    What Is Digital Humanities and What's It Doing in English Departments?

    Matthew Kirschenbaum, in Debates in the Digital Humanities, ed. Matthew K. Gold (University of Minnesota Press, 2012), pp. 3–11. We read this in class between 29 October and 9 November 2026.
    Annotated essayAnalysisSummary of learning

    Annotated essay

    8 pages

    I worked through the essay one paragraph at a time. Main ideas are in blue. Red marks anything that links back to class, such as concordances, word frequency, metadata and literary mapping. Arrows connect later sections to earlier ones. Tap a page to open it full size.

    Analysis

    A definition borrowed from Wikipedia

    Kirschenbaum never gives his own definition of digital humanities. He quotes Wikipedia's and says it is good enough. Then he checks the page's edit history and finds that DH scholars wrote it. I starred this in the margin. The field is describing itself on a page anyone can edit, and the people describing it are the people doing it. Drucker's point from class is that data is always chosen by someone. The same applies to a definition.

    What he offers instead is a history of the name. In 2001 Blackwell's editors wanted to call their book A Companion to Digitized Humanities. John Unsworth argued for "digital", because "digitized" suggested little more than scanning. ADHO followed in 2005, the NEH's Digital Humanities Initiative in 2006, and the NEH Office of Digital Humanities in 2008. So the name was settled before the field was. A title chosen partly with marketing in mind ended up naming a discipline.

    Twitter and the 2009 MLA

    The middle section turns to the 2009 MLA convention. Amanda French found that nearly half the people at the DH conference that year were tweeting, compared with 3 percent at MLA. Kirschenbaum describes the picture Twitter gives of the field as a network topology, and I wrote "who follows whom" beside it. He is using a DH method, network mapping, to describe DH itself.

    The Brian Croxall story shifts the focus from tools to people. Croxall could not afford to travel to the convention, so his paper was read in his absence and posted on his blog. It became the most-read paper of the convention. In this part of the essay, DH becomes a way of talking about academic jobs, open access and who owns research. That partly answers Alan Liu, who argues that DH says too little about power. In Kirschenbaum's account, people were already using the label to protest.

    Why English departments

    His first reason for DH's place in English departments is simple: after numbers, text is the easiest kind of data for a computer to process. I linked this in red to our class list of reasons for using computers in literary study. I already do some of this every day. Searching a PDF with Ctrl+F is a concordance, and my yearly music summary is a frequency count.

    I would question the essay at the same point where Kirschenbaum questions it himself. In a note he admits that it "wears its disciplinary bias on its sleeve", since it deals with English departments at large public universities in the US. Reading it in Bengaluru, I thought of Bichitra, which has put around 140,000 pages of Tagore online. The essay explains a lot about DH. It also made me think about who tells the story of a field, and from where.

    LO1 debates on naming, labour and open accessLO2 text analysis, networks, archives in literature and media

    Summary of learning

    In my words

    • DH is where questions from literature, history and culture meet computational methods. The influence runs both ways. Computers change how we read, and the humanities study what computers do to us.
    • The field chose "digital" over "digitized" because its work goes beyond copying books. It also involves searching, counting, mapping and interpreting them.
    • DH grew through people as much as tools. Twitter, blogs and conferences helped it see itself as a field.
    • The label is political. It is connected to open access, ownership of research and academic labour.
    • Someone chooses every dataset, and every definition too, so it is worth asking who chose them.

    In Kirschenbaum's words

    "to shift the emphasis away from simple digitization"John Unsworth, quoted on p. 5

    "more akin to a common methodological outlook"p. 4

    "a network topology"p. 8

    "collaborative and depend on networks of people"p. 9

    Down the Drain

    Where we walked on 25 November

    Site A Lake Verandahs, Hiranandani, Akshaya Nagar West 3:07 to 3:22 pm
    Site B Mahaveer Ridge and Radiant Shine, Begur side 3:50 to 3:55 pm

    Project descriptionRationaleVariablesData collectionIRB and ethical clearanceObjectives and outcomesSocial impact and research valueDH concepts and locatednessPhoto archiveSources

    The project

    We want to build a layered digital map of two apartment complexes near our campus. Each point on the map will be a piece of waste or water infrastructure: a bin, a bin room, a stormwater grating, a floor drain, a sewage channel or a patch of standing water. Every point will carry a photograph and our field notes. Where staff and residents agree to talk to us, it will also carry what they tell us. The rules that apply to these places, and the area's history of flooding, will be added as further layers.

    The two sites are quite different. Lake Verandahs (Site A) is a large high-rise township with covered basements. The blocks around Mahaveer Ridge and Radiant Shine (Site B) are smaller, with open driveways and a separate bin room. Comparing them lets us ask whether a building's size and design affect how it handles waste and water.

    While planning this I kept thinking of Leonia in Calvino's Invisible Cities, a city that renews itself every day while its rubbish collects outside the walls. Gated complexes are arranged in a similar way. The lawn and lobby face the street, and the bins and drains are kept out of sight. This project looks at what is kept out of sight.

    How I understand it

    Before our first visit I didn't expect drains to tell us much. The basement at Lake Verandahs changed my mind. The smell from the sewage channel was strong enough that all four of us covered our noses, and we took a photo of it. The parts of the complex that residents and visitors see are designed to look good. The basement isn't designed for anyone to look at. For me, the project is about recording those hidden parts of the city and using a map to show them next to the parts people usually see.

    Why this project, and why now

    4kinds of waste every home must now keep apart: wet, dry, sanitary and special care, under the Solid Waste Management Rules 2026, in force since April
    ~2,000of about 50,000 bulk waste generators in Bengaluru have the vendor arrangements the rules require
    860 kmof major stormwater drains across about 633 catchments, often choked with garbage and silt
    800+houses flooded when the Hulimavu lake bund breached on 24 November 2019, close to our sites

    The topic is current. Bengaluru's new Solid Waste Management Rules came into force in April 2026. Every household must now separate four kinds of waste, and BSWML, the city's waste company, has said it will stop collecting mixed waste. Large apartment complexes carry more of the responsibility under a new idea called Extended Bulk Waste Generator Responsibility. We want to see how these rules are being followed on the ground.

    Waste and drainage are closely linked. After heavy rain, news reports describe the same sequence: garbage blocks the drains, water can't get away, and roads and basements flood, sometimes with sewage. We saw small signs of this on our walk. Petals and leaves were caught in a grating, a puddle was still standing well after the rain, and a basement channel smelt strongly of sewage.

    The sites are also close to home. Both are in 560076, the same PIN code as our campus. In November 2019 the bund of Hulimavu lake, which had been taking in sewage from upstream, breached and flooded hundreds of homes in this area. Our walk took place almost exactly seven years later. Since we pass these places regularly, we can go back, check what we find and stay accountable to the people involved.

    The rules have also changed often. The threshold for a bulk waste generator has moved from 20 flats to 50 and then to 100, and the requirements for apartment sewage treatment plants have been tightened and relaxed more than once. A record of what actually exists on site adds evidence to a debate that mostly happens on paper.

    What we will record

    These are the variables we will record at each site. Every observation is linked to a point on the map.

    VariableWhat we recordHow

    How we will collect data

      All our tools are free. We will use GPS Map Camera for photos, a shared spreadsheet for the data, uMap or QGIS with OpenStreetMap for the map, Google Forms for the survey, Voyant Tools to look for repeated words in interview transcripts, and this website to publish the results.

      The pilot walk showed us the limits of photographs. Drains, bins and standing water were easy to record. Collection times, how the smell changes during the day and what happens in heavy rain were not, because only the people who work there know these things. Interviews will be an important part of the project.

      Ethics and IRB clearance

      Our project involves the people who handle waste, so ethics matters. Because we will survey and interview people, we need approval from Christ University's Research Conduct and Ethics Committee (RCEC), which is the university's Institutional Review Board. We will apply using the student ethics form, with our course coordinator as supervisor. No surveys or interviews will take place before we have approval.

      Permissions

      • Written permission from each residents' association or facility manager before further visits, especially to basements, bin rooms and service areas
      • Approval of the topic from our course coordinator
      • Informed consent, in English and Kannada, from every survey respondent and interviewee

      Protecting participants

      • Housekeeping and waste staff are employed by the people who manage these sites, which puts them in a vulnerable position. They will stay anonymous. We will not photograph their faces or share what they say with their employers.
      • Waste work in India is linked to caste. We will not ask about caste or record anything that could reveal it.
      • Published photos will not show residents, flat numbers, number plates or name boards. Anything caught by accident will be blurred.
      • The only people in our photos are group members, and all of us agreed to appear.

      Survey responses will be anonymous and stored on our university Google accounts. We will name the complexes on this site only if their associations agree; otherwise we will call them Site A and Site B. We want to understand how the system works and don't intend to single out one building. If we find a safety hazard, such as an open manhole, we will report it privately to the association first.

      Objectives and outcomes

      Objectives

      • Map every waste and water point we can access at both sites, with photos and notes
      • Compare the 2026 waste rules and the sewage rules with what we observe
      • Record how staff and residents experience the system, including smell, flooding and collection
      • Place each site in the local history of drains, lakes and flooding
      • Find out whether students using free tools can produce a useful civic map

      Outcomes

      • An interactive layered map of both sites, published on this website
      • A photo archive in which each image keeps its location, time and photographer
      • A short essay comparing the two sites
      • A one-page guide to the four waste streams for residents, shared with the associations
      • An open dataset that citizen groups auditing Bengaluru's drains can reuse

      Why it matters

      For residents, the map can show where segregation breaks down and which drains block first. Fixing these problems before the monsoon costs less than dealing with a flood afterwards, and associations can use the evidence with BSWML, waste vendors or the water board.

      The project also records what housekeeping and waste staff know about these buildings, which is rarely written down. We will do this carefully and with their consent.

      As research, it adds detailed local data where most information is city-wide, held by government or hard to access. Our data will be open, and it can sit alongside citizen work such as the Mod Foundation's guided drain audits and OpenCity's stormwater datajam of May 2026. It also covers private gated land, which public audits usually cannot reach.

      Where this sits in DH

      Most of our course readings deal with texts, so a project on drains might seem far from English. The methods carry over, though. Close reading becomes close observation, like noticing petals in a grating the way we would notice an unusual word in a poem. Distant reading becomes the map, where many small observations add up to a pattern. Kirschenbaum's description of DH as collaborative and tied to infrastructure fits this project closely, since it is four students studying a city's infrastructure with digital tools and sharing the results openly.

      Photo archive

      25 Nov 2026

      Our group took all of these photos with GPS Map Camera, an app that adds the place, coordinates and time to each image. We kept the stamps because the metadata is part of the record. The numbers match the points on the map.
